extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and historians of science; readers of Popular Science Monthly interested in scientific biography and practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and standards embodied in the biography of Charles Lyell that describe what makes a competent or exemplary modern geologist (methods, habits, attitudes, and professional practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel and field observation as primary requisites
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must preach up traveling, as Demosthenes did delivery, as the first, second, and third requisites for a modern geologist.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyell 'ran up and down and to and fro upon the face of the earth, inspecting its crust everywhere,' his letters are 'full of his observations taken in on the spot.' The text uses his extensive travel (Isle of Wight, Paris basin, Lyme Regis, Sicily, Pyrenees, Eifel, Scandinavia, America, etc.) as evidence that seeing things firsthand is central to geological competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of reasoning: use causes now acting (actualism/uniformitarianism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyell's plan: 'that no causes whatever have, from the earliest time to which we can look back, to the present, ever acted, but those now acting; and that they never acted with different degrees of energy from that which they now exert.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Principles of Geology' aims to establish a method of reasoning in the science based on present causes explaining the past; this methodological stance is presented as a core standard for geological interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original observation over second-hand authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of others: 'we have by our joint tour fathomed the depth and ascertained the shallowness of the geologists of France as to their original observations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises first-hand fieldwork and original observations and contrasts them with reliance on second-hand memoirs; Lyell's travels and direct inspections are held up as superior practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devotion to the work and independence from monetary motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyell's own declaration: 'I shall never hope to make money by geology' and 'I will waste no time in book-making for lucre's sake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The biography treats wholehearted devotion—sparing no expense or trouble to render oneself competent—and refusal to prioritize financial reward as a professional and moral standard for serious scientific work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to new facts and readiness to incorporate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated characterization: 'Lyell's ears are open for everything new in the geological line from the ends of the earth inward.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyell's letters 'teem with new facts or discoveries.' The text uses this to emphasize that a good geologist keeps attentive to new evidence from diverse places and sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn languages and study foreign literature/places
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Their language must be learned; the places to which their memoirs relate, visited;'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that to properly evaluate foreign geologists' work one must learn the language and visit the field sites; Lyell learned languages (French, Italian, German, some Spanish) and visited study localities as part of rigorous scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth of culture and interdisciplinary curiosity (catholicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyell is described as 'very catholic' in interests — attending art, poetry, music, philosophy and mixing in cultivated society as well as scientific circles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats wide intellectual sympathy (letters on poetry, art, politics, social life) as a valuable trait that complements technical scientific work rather than narrowing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keen eye for talent and networking with peers
rubrics_metrics.description: 'His eye for men was very keen' — he recognized and predicted figures like Huxley, Geikie, Agassiz.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lyell's ability to identify promising scientists and to correspond and mix with leading intellects is presented as part of effective scientific leadership and mentorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful, cautious intellectual stance toward new theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding Darwin: 'he formally rejected the theory as broached by Lamarck, and he hesitated for some time to accept [Darwin]; he was but a lukewarm convert.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The biography frames measured skepticism—reserving judgment until evidence accumulates—as a professional virtue; acceptance of new paradigms should be cautious and evidence-based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incrementalism: value the cumulative effect of small changes ('infinitesimal')
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyell 'was to be one of the first to discover the cumulative value of the infinitesimal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on slow, gradual processes (and building arguments from many small observations) rather than sudden cataclysms is presented as a methodological preference and evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize original research over institutional position when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyell accepted and then vacated a professorship because 'it interfered with his schemes of traveling and original research.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises choosing active field research and original contribution over holding office that would limit one's capacity to do primary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extensive correspondence and publication to advance scientific reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: His review of Scrope and the plan for the 'Principles' show he aimed 'to establish the principle of reasoning in the science' and he maintained wide correspondence with figures (Humboldt, Darwin, Ticknor, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The biography highlights publishing influential syntheses and maintaining broad correspondence as ways to disseminate methodology and shape the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and sociological awareness when interpreting observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lyell judged American political and social institutions with attention to factors like abundant land, immigration, and local circumstances affecting institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text commends interpreting observational data within its broader social and environmental context rather than making naive cross-cultural generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance empirical focus with general culture and humane sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although rigorous in geology, Lyell retained 'general culture'—interest in art, literature, and social life—and this is said to have 'left some good effects' in his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests that combining empirical rigor with wider cultural engagement produces better scientists and better writing (e.g., his letters and popular works).
